lessons.title: Growth vs Value, and Large Cap vs Small/Midcap Across the Cycle

body.text: Sector is not the only lens on equities. Two more dials, growth versus value, and large cap versus small/midcap, rotate with the cycle too, and interest rates are the hinge that swings both of them at once.

children.text: The last lesson rotated leadership between sectors. This lesson cuts the same market two other ways: by style, growth stocks versus value stocks, and by size, large caps versus small and midcaps. Both dimensions overlap heavily with sector rotation, but they deserve their own treatment because the single biggest lever behind both, interest rates, works through a slightly different mechanism than the sector story does.
Growth vs Value: Two Ways to Pay for a Business

columns.label: Growth stocks
points: Priced mainly on earnings expected several years out
High P/E, low or no dividend, most profit reinvested
Examples: fast-scaling internet and consumer businesses, some private banks and insurers early in their growth curve
The bet is on the size and certainty of future cash flows

columns.label: Value stocks
points: Priced mainly on earnings already being made now
Low P/E relative to current or historical earnings, often higher dividends
Examples: PSU banks, PSU commodity producers, metal and mining companies
The bet is that the market is underpaying for cash flows already in hand

children.text: Why Rising Rates Hurt Growth Stocks More

markDefs.definition: How sensitive an asset's present value is to a change in the discount rate (interest rate) used to value its future cash flows. A cash flow far in the future has higher duration, and is more sensitive, than a cash flow arriving soon.

children.text: Every share price is, at heart, today's value of a stream of future cash flows, discounted back at some interest rate. A growth stock's value sits mostly in cash flows many years out. A value stock's value sits mostly in cash flows arriving soon. This gives growth stocks a much higher equity
, the same concept you'll meet again with bonds in the next chapter. When interest rates rise, far-future cash flows lose far more of their present value than near-term ones do.

body.caption: Present value of a single future cash flow (CF), discounted at rate r over n years
Same ₹100 cash flow, same 2-percentage-point rate rise (8% to 10%), very different impact

body.text: The same 2-percentage-point rate move erases about 17% of the value of a cash flow 10 years out, roughly eight times the roughly 2% it takes off a cash flow due in a year. This is the mechanism behind a very real Indian episode: through 2022, as the RBI and other central banks raised rates sharply, several richly valued new-age internet businesses that had listed on the exchanges saw their share prices fall by 60 to 80% from their highs, even as their revenues kept growing, while PSU banks and PSU commodity companies, priced on near-term earnings, staged a strong multi-year rally over the same stretch.

body.title: Calculate the Duration Effect
body.prompt: A cash flow of ₹100 is expected in 5 years. Using the same rate move as the table above, from 8% to 10%, by approximately what percentage does its present value fall? Enter your answer as a positive number.
body.explanation: PV at 8% = 100 ÷ 1.08^5 ≈ ₹68.1. PV at 10% = 100 ÷ 1.10^5 ≈ ₹62.1. Fall = (68.1 − 62.1) ÷ 68.1 ≈ 8.8%. Notice it sits neatly between the roughly 2% fall for a 1-year cash flow and the roughly 17% fall for a 10-year one; longer duration means a bigger fall for the same rate move.

children.text: Large Cap vs Small/Midcap: The Size Dimension

Small and midcap stocks tend to be more domestic, more leveraged to local demand, and more dependent on easy liquidity and risk appetite than large caps. That makes them the biggest beneficiaries when a recovery gets underway, and among the most vulnerable when risk appetite disappears. Large caps, with stronger balance sheets and deeper institutional ownership, tend to fall less in a downturn and are usually the first place investors hide within equities without leaving the asset class altogether.

body.title: Same three indices, opposite phases of the cycle (approximate, rounded returns)

body.text: Same three indices, completely opposite outcomes, one cycle apart. In FY21's recovery, smallcaps outgained the Nifty 50 by roughly 50 percentage points. In CY2018's slowdown, triggered by the IL&FS default and a mutual fund recategorisation-led selloff, smallcaps underperformed the Nifty 50 by nearly 30 percentage points in the other direction. "Small and midcap" is not a permanently higher-return bet, it is a higher-beta bet whose outcome depends entirely on which phase you're in when you hold it.

Watch for a repeat setup. In February and March 2024, after a strong multi-year run in small and midcap stocks, SEBI directed AMFI to have small and midcap mutual fund schemes run liquidity stress tests and disclose the results, flagging concerns about stretched valuations and how easily these schemes could meet redemptions in a sharp downturn. A long run of small/midcap outperformance does not mean the phase has changed forever, it can just as easily mean the setup for the next CY2018-style correction is quietly building.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: The RBI unexpectedly signals a longer period of higher interest rates than the market had priced in. All else equal, the framework in this lesson would expect this to hurt which combination the most?
options: Nothing, interest rates don't affect equity valuations
body.explanation: Growth stocks carry the highest equity duration, so their far-future cash flows lose the most present value when rates rise. Small and midcaps, being more liquidity- and risk-appetite-sensitive, tend to compound that effect, since a "higher rates for longer" signal usually also cools the broader risk appetite they depend on.

body.title: A Familiar-Looking Peak
body.scenario: Small and midcap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 for three straight years. Valuations on standard metrics like P/E and P/B are well above their 10-year averages for both indices. Mutual fund inflows into small and midcap schemes have been at record highs for several months, and some fund houses have started restricting fresh lump-sum inflows into their smallcap funds.
body.prompt: Using what you've learned about growth versus value, size, and the earlier phase-mapping lessons, what phase does this setup most resemble, and what would make you cautious?
body.modelAnswer: This combination, a long run of small/midcap outperformance, stretched valuations, record inflows, and fund houses restricting new money, closely resembles the conditions that preceded the CY2018 correction: strength that has run long enough and hard enough to attract late, valuation-insensitive money, with early signs (fund restrictions) that the froth is being recognised from inside the industry. It does not tell you the exact quarter a correction starts, corrections can be delayed by continued strong earnings or fresh liquidity, but it is exactly the kind of setup where a large-cap tilt, more resilient balance sheets, deeper liquidity, becomes a more comfortable place to sit within equities, even without leaving the asset class.

cards.definition: A stock priced mainly on earnings expected several years out, typically carrying a high P/E and high equity duration.
A stock priced mainly on earnings already being generated now, typically carrying a lower P/E and lower equity duration.
How sensitive a stock's present value is to a change in interest rates; higher for stocks whose value depends more on far-future cash flows.
Smaller-market-capitalisation stocks, generally more domestic, more liquidity-sensitive, and higher-beta than large caps.

body.text: Index returns, valuation levels, and dates in this lesson are rounded, approximate, and drawn from widely reported figures, provided for education only. The present value calculations use simplified, illustrative discount rates and are not a valuation model for any specific stock. Nothing here is investment advice; consult a SEBI registered investment adviser for advice on your own portfolio.

points: Growth stocks are priced mainly on far-future earnings and carry high equity duration; value stocks are priced mainly on current earnings and carry low equity duration
A given rise in interest rates cuts far more off the present value of a far-future cash flow than a near-term one, which is why rate hikes hit growth stocks harder than value stocks
The 2022 rate-hiking cycle saw richly valued new-age internet stocks fall sharply while PSU banks and commodity producers rallied, a real-world duration effect
Small and midcaps are a higher-beta bet on the cycle, not a permanently higher-return one: they led by a wide margin in FY21's recovery and lagged by a wide margin in CY2018's slowdown
A long run of small/midcap outperformance with stretched valuations and record inflows, as seen again in 2023-24, echoes the setup that preceded the CY2018 correction and deserves extra caution
Style (growth/value) and size (large/small) rotate with the cycle much like sectors do, and interest rates are the common thread driving both
